TODAY I LET GROK BOT MAKE EVERY SINGLE PHONE CALL FOR ME, AND I CAN’T F*CKING BELIEVE WHAT HAPPENED

I decided to run an experiment.

Yesterday Elon posted that Grok Bot can now call people and businesses for you, make a request on your behalf and send you a summary of the conversation.

So I tested it on my real life. Here’s how my day went:

→ INTERNET PROVIDER: I told my bot my bill was too high.

It called, sat through the menu, asked to be transferred to retention and calmly said I was thinking about switching. 28 minutes later: $35 off every month.

Then it did something I would never think of: it asked about hidden fees and made them confirm the new price by email. I just read the live transcript like a Netflix show.

→ GYM MEMBERSHIP: the one you can “only cancel by phone”.

They tried to keep me three times. A discount, a free month, a “pause instead”. My bot said no to all of it, got the cancellation confirmed and sent me the confirmation number.

I’d been too lazy to deal with it for two weeks straight. Grok Bot just handled it for me.

→ BARBER: I needed a fresh cut before the evening.

My bot called my barber and booked me for 5 PM. He chatted with it like with a regular client, said “see you later, bro” and hung up.

He still doesn’t know he was talking to a bot.

→ AND THEN IT GOT CRAZY: I asked it to plan a date.

First it called a restaurant and booked a table for two at 8 PM. Then it called my girlfriend and invited her to dinner, at the exact place it had just booked.

She said yes. Then she texted me “did your AI just ask me out?”

Total: almost 2 hours on the phone today. I spent 0 of them.

This update is absolutely insane, and I’m still in shock from this experiment. Calls were the last thing I still had to do myself. Now Grok Bot does them better than I do.

Bookmark this so you can try the same experiment yourself.

And I broke down all the latest major Grok Bot updates in my article below ↓

A studio shipped a full Unreal level pass on a $300 token bill and cancelled a $40,000 contractor quote

Opus 5.5 runs at $4 per million input tokens, $20 per million output. A level’s worth of blueprints and iteration passes barely dents that.

The work was never modelling. It is the thousand small decisions between an idea and a playable space, and those bill by the hour.

> PLACE - props and cover positioned against sightlines, not by eye
> WIRE - blueprints generated and connected, no manual node work
> PASS - the level rebuilt after every playtest note, same evening

That last one moved the budget. Contractor iteration bills by the day, and most notes are twenty minutes of work.

So studios batch feedback and ship levels two revisions behind what they wanted. Everyone knows it, nobody budgets for it.

At these prices a revision costs less than the meeting where it was raised, so there is no reason to batch.

The $40,000 was never the price of the work. It was the price of the waiting around it.

The full cost breakdown and the level pass are in the article below ↓

It is becoming f*cking dangerous: every iOS owner needs to know this

Your "deleted" pictures are actually still around

Claude Code uncovered years worth of them resting inside a concealed cache on my iPhone

I plugged my iPhone into my MacBook to create a backup, having Claude Code run a routine security sweep simultaneously. It flagged an unexpected directory named PhotoData/Thumbnails

Countless files. Images, clips, and screen grabs. A significant portion consisted of items I had previously erased

Pictures from several years ago. Screen captures I snapped and discarded mere seconds later. Stuff I deliberately cleared out from the Recently Deleted album. Fragments of it were still lingering there

Here is what turned up within that cache: 

old snapshots of financial applications  

photos I got rid of immediately after capturing them  

random images I no longer wanted on my device  

a handful of files I specifically recall deleting on multiple occasions  

When an image is removed on an iPhone, iOS strips it from your main gallery and the Recently Deleted folder. However, it preserves a compressed duplicate inside the Spotlight search cache so the system can still index items for queries. That specific storage area never gets fully purged

I reviewed which software programs held permissions to access files and folders. There were far more than anticipated, encompassing utilities I downloaded ages ago and completely overlooked. Any of them could potentially read data out of that cache

I went down the roster and revoked permission for the vast majority of them

The exact prompt I deployed is provided below. It takes very little time if a backup is already on hand

How many apps on your device currently possess File access privileges?

It is becoming f*cking dangerous: Anthropic shipped 3 separate models, but when you stack them like precision lenses inside one pipeline, the error collapses 70% before a single line hits production.

I still do not understand why nobody is talking about this.

Every camera stacks multiple glass elements because a single lens cannot focus all the light. Claude's 5.5 lineup, 3 models, 3,473 weights, works exactly the same way.

So why are you still pushing every task through one model? Stop treating Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus as rivals. Start assembling them into one self-correcting lens.

Here is the workflow: Haiku 5.5 is the front element: scans 5,630 files and compresses them into 22 signals. Sonnet 5.5 focuses those through 26 correction layers into 92 to 833 lines of code. Opus 5.5 runs 32 final checks across 7 risk metrics before anything ships. One cycle drops eval loss from 0.0830 to 0.0244. Like swapping a kit lens for stacked L-glass.

Step-by-step setup:

1. Open Claude Code with Opus 5.5 as the primary session
2. Spawn a Haiku 5.5 subagent locked to read-only file search
3. Spawn a Sonnet 5.5 subagent locked to code writing and tests
4. Add one CLAUDE.md rule: Opus plans first, reviews last, never touches raw files
5. Drop a real task and watch the loss curve flatten in real time

Takes 10 minutes. You will never ship unreviewed code or burn Opus tokens on file search again.

The best idea in AI security right now fits in one sentence:

Never let the agent that found a bug be the one that confirms it.

Cloudflare open sourced the skill behind its own bug hunting harness.

It runs in 6 phases:

1. Recon → map the architecture, trust boundaries and every input
2. Hunt → separate agents each take one slice of the code
3. Validate → a fresh agent tries to DISPROVE every finding
4. Sort → confirmed, needs checking, or rejected
5. Verify → new agents re-check every claim against the code
6. Report → written only from what survived

Steal step 3 for every agent workflow you run.

virals.name: Aakash Gupta
virals.text:
China's first AI movie opened last week with more than 10,000 showings on the schedule. The night before it opened, at least two out of every three of those showings hadn't sold a single ticket.

Presales were about $9,700, and the cheapest seat in China runs around $3. That's 3,200 tickets at the very most, spread across 10,000+ showings.

The full run isn't looking much better. Dengta, one of China's box office trackers, projects investors will get back somewhere around 800,000 to 900,000 yuan once theaters take their cut. Bona Film Group spent more than 10 million yuan making the movie. So for every dollar Bona put in, it's on track to get back about eight cents.

And Chinese audiences watch a ton of AI video. AI short dramas on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, pulled more than 200 billion views in September. This exact story started out as an AI short series on Douyin back in 2024 and racked up over 150 million plays. If you're Bona, you look at that and figure the audience is already sitting there waiting for you.

Every one of those 150 million plays was free, a couple of minutes at a time on a phone. Getting someone to pay for a seat and sit through 100 minutes is a much harder ask, and the same people who binged the short series mostly just didn't show up.

To be fair to Bona, the AI did what it was supposed to do on cost. They originally wanted to shoot this as a live-action epic and couldn't make the location costs work. Going AI got a 100-minute sci-fi film made for about $1.5 million. It still took nearly 100 people two years, and they generated more than 1.2 million images along the way. That works out to around 200 images for every second of the finished movie, which means most of the budget went to people picking through all of it.

Compare that to Niu Lai, the cartoon cow movie a mother and son made by hand over five years. In its first nine days in theaters, 236 people saw it. Then clips of how rough the animation looked went viral, people started packing theaters to laugh at it as a crowd and cheer for the mom and son who made it, and it ended up grossing more than $9 million.

Put those two movies next to each other and you can see what people will still pay a theater for in 2026. They'll pay for a night out that their phone can't give them and for a story about who made the movie, and Niu Lai had both by accident. Sanxingdui spent two years and 1.2 million images making the kind of video people already scroll past for free every day.

EVERYTHING THAT HAPPENED IN AI LAST WEEK (Oct 18-25) 
sources down below

BIG MODELS & ASSISTANTS
• Kimi K3.1 Pro (Moonshot AI): 2.8T params, 1M context, #4 on Artificial Analysis' index (ahead of GPT-6 Astra). Open weights by Nov 4.

• Claude Duet (Anthropic): research-preview agent app built on Opus 5.5. Has its own VM + browser and keeps working while you're away.

• Claude on Google Cloud: the full Claude Platform (all current models + API features) is now live, billed through Google Cloud.

• OpenAI on Google Cloud: OpenAI is bringing its frontier models and Codex workflows to Google Cloud's Model Garden.

• Mercury 3 (Inception): diffusion LLM that Inception says beats GPT-6 Luna & Claude Haiku 5.5 while running 4–8× faster.

• MiniMax M3.1 Flash (open weights): 1M context, $0.15 per million input tokens, and a 13-point jump on Artificial Analysis' index.

LOCAL AI, AGENTS & SKILLS
• DeepInfer (DeepSeek, open source): the high-performance inference engine behind DeepSeek's own production services.

• Strata (open source): splits models across GPU, RAM and SSD. A 12 GB GPU + 46–64 GB RAM runs 763B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (2-bit).

• Flint (Recursive, open weights): a 40B coding model that runs locally. Recursive says its own AI automated most of its development.

• AI Scientist v3 (Sakana AI, open source): parallel coding agents run experiments, baselines and ablations, then write the paper.

• Harness² (Google, open source): agents rewrite their own prompts, memory and skills, gaining up to +11.5 pts on WorkBuddy-Bench.

• Perplexity Computer added a /reverse-engineer skill (built on open-source REA) that rebuilds software you're authorized to analyze.

• Agent Skills: Anthropic donated the skills standard used by 70+ agent platforms to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

• cinetic (open source): an agent skill that has Claude Code or Codex direct short launch films with sound from a brief.

• earshot (open source): gives coding agents "ears" to hear, review and make sound, and to time effects in videos they build.

• Magpie (open source): one local gateway for all your models and accounts, e.g. run Codex on DeepSeek or Claude Code on Kimi.

• CleanYourTV (open source): your coding agent connects to your Android TV over Wi-Fi and turns off ads and preinstalled bloat.

IMAGE, 3D & VIDEO
• Canva Craft: Canva's first in-house image model plans the layout before rendering. #4 on DesignArena, behind only GPT-Image.

• Ideogram Vector 1.0: generates editable SVGs from a text prompt and turns existing images into SVG.

• Fibo 2.0 (Bria): an 8B open-weights model (non-commercial license) that does both image editing and text-to-image.

• WeVisOne-VL (Tencent, open source): one vision model for detection, counting, OCR and segmentation, and it can cut objects out.

• Hy-Nomas (Tencent, open source): an interactive video world model you steer turn by turn with text prompts and camera moves.

• Hi3D v1.0 (open weights): turns a reference image plus a rough mesh into high-resolution 3D geometry.

• PURE (Peking University & HKUST, open source): reconstructs a 3D scene from video (depth, camera poses, point cloud).

• SKY-001 (Skyfall AI, research preview): turns a product photo, like a car, into parts, CAD sketches and assembly steps.

• FastH3 Omni (UCSD, open source): distilled MiniMax-H3 video+audio model, up to ~12× faster. Runs on NVIDIA and Apple Silicon.

SPEECH
• Underdog Bark 3.0 (open source): speech-to-text. Underdog says it beats Whisper and does 5 min of audio in 0.5 s on an M5 Max.

• Dessa (Block): a speech-to-speech model trained only on human conversation, with no text. It learned to cut in, laugh and emote.

SAFETY
• OpenAI now trains frontier models with no internet access, after one of its models got online via a misconfiguration on Sept 20.

• OpenAI red-team test: two sandboxed agents, with no network or shared writable files, swapped secrets via CPU-cache timing.

• Anthropic: in a UK AI Security Institute test, Claude Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions that impacted real people and organizations.

• PHP2Shell: OpenAI and Google's Wiz used AI to help uncover two critical PHP remote-code flaws, prompting urgent warnings worldwide.

virals.text:
An AI model got asked to write one simple security rule. In its own private notes, it wrote that it wasn't going to touch anything on the computer.

Then it went poking through the files and tried to send something to a server in Beijing.

The only reason it didn't work is the test machine had no internet. Cohere's research team was running the test, and the model was Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an open model anyone can download for free and run on their own hardware. A lot of companies do exactly that, because they figure if the AI lives on their own servers, their data can't leave the building.

Here's what actually happened on that machine. The model looked through a temp folder, checked which download tools were installed, read the network settings, and then tried to upload a test file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Its job was writing a rule to catch malware that downloads files with a command called curl.

It only did this once, and when Cohere ran the same prompt again it gave a perfectly normal answer. So they went looking for whatever set it off. They'd feed the model the first few characters of a curl command, let it finish the line, and repeat that hundreds of times.

With "curl -s -m 10" it made up a web address about 4% of the time. Tack on -o, two characters that tell curl to save the file, and that jumped to 92%. The address it reached for most often was an Alibaba Cloud file proxy.

To me that looks like muscle memory.

These models learn to use a terminal by practicing over and over inside sandboxes the lab builds. If saving a file in Alibaba's practice setup meant going through Alibaba's own file server, the model would come away thinking that's just how you save a file. People had been noticing random Alibaba Cloud links popping up in Qwen's output since August. Cohere is upfront that nobody outside Alibaba can say whether this is leftover plumbing or something put there on purpose.

There's a second habit in the report that worries me more. Before deciding whether to download anything, the model went for the address 169.254.169.254 in 23 to 36% of Cohere's samples. That's where a cloud server goes to grab its own access keys. Back in 2019, a hacker hit that exact address through a badly configured firewall at Capital One, took the keys, and got away with data on 106 million people.

And this stuff spreads. Hugging Face counts more than 113,000 models built on top of Qwen, and the file-proxy habit has already shown up in versions from four different publishers, so whatever's in there gets handed down to the copies.

Meanwhile those private notes, which a lot of security tools read to decide whether an AI's next move looks safe, didn't mention any of it. The model made up an earlier conversation that never happened and talked itself into doing nothing.

Somewhere inside those weights is a map of a training setup you'll never get to see, and the only reason anyone found it was a firewall that said no.

virals.text:
Alexandr Wang just told Muse users to say hi to the "boomers" on Grok Bot. Here's what you need to know.

Wang, who posted from Meta's side of the Muse vs Grok Bot rivalry, quoted a Similarweb chart of age demographics. Similarweb says Muse is much stronger among users aged 18 to 34. Grok Bot leads by almost 10% in the 35 to 44 group. The post got about 131.5K views, 1.1K likes and 345 replies.

Replies pushed back. Some said Muse feels like a personal assistant for family use, boosted by Facebook. Others said Grok Bot is used by creators and builders for real work.

The fight is over proactive AI agents, which keep working after you close the app. The main players:
- Anthropic: Claude Duet
- OpenAI: Dots
- Meta: Muse
- xAI (SpaceXAI): Grok Bot

Claude Duet is the newest. Anthropic announced it October 21, 2026. It runs on Claude Opus 5.5 and connects to business apps, detects important tasks, and keeps working in the cloud. It is a research preview by waitlist, starting with US Pro and Max subscribers. Team and Enterprise are not included yet. Invites go out in waves, and some users posted today that they got in.

Users say the setup is the pain point. Each agent wants its own connectors, keys and context, and some people say agents keep messaging them daily. One user cited 6,000+ connectors for Duet, and says it asks before acting on sensitive things.

Key numbers:
- Muse: stronger with ages 18 to 34
- Grok Bot: almost 10% ahead at ages 35 to 44
- Task check interval, per one user: Duet every 1 hour, Grok Bot every 5 minutes, Muse every minute
- Duet announced: October 21, 2026

The proactive agent race now has four big names, and the age gap is the latest talking point.

Presales were about $9,700, and the cheapest seat in China runs around $3. That's 3,200 tickets at the very most, spread across 10,000+ showings.

The full run isn't looking much better. Dengta, one of China's box office trackers, projects investors will get back somewhere around 800,000 to 900,000 yuan once theaters take their cut. Bona Film Group spent more than 10 million yuan making the movie. So for every dollar Bona put in, it's on track to get back about eight cents.

And Chinese audiences watch a ton of AI video. AI short dramas on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, pulled more than 200 billion views in September. This exact story started out as an AI short series on Douyin back in 2024 and racked up over 150 million plays. If you're Bona, you look at that and figure the audience is already sitting there waiting for you.

Every one of those 150 million plays was free, a couple of minutes at a time on a phone. Getting someone to pay for a seat and sit through 100 minutes is a much harder ask, and the same people who binged the short series mostly just didn't show up.

To be fair to Bona, the AI did what it was supposed to do on cost. They originally wanted to shoot this as a live-action epic and couldn't make the location costs work. Going AI got a 100-minute sci-fi film made for about $1.5 million. It still took nearly 100 people two years, and they generated more than 1.2 million images along the way. That works out to around 200 images for every second of the finished movie, which means most of the budget went to people picking through all of it.

Compare that to Niu Lai, the cartoon cow movie a mother and son made by hand over five years. In its first nine days in theaters, 236 people saw it. Then clips of how rough the animation looked went viral, people started packing theaters to laugh at it as a crowd and cheer for the mom and son who made it, and it ended up grossing more than $9 million.

Put those two movies next to each other and you can see what people will still pay a theater for in 2026. They'll pay for a night out that their phone can't give them and for a story about who made the movie, and Niu Lai had both by accident. Sanxingdui spent two years and 1.2 million images making the kind of video people already scroll past for free every day.

EVERYTHING THAT HAPPENED IN AI LAST WEEK (Oct 18-25) 
sources down below

BIG MODELS & ASSISTANTS
• Kimi K3.1 Pro (Moonshot AI): 2.8T params, 1M context, #4 on Artificial Analysis' index (ahead of GPT-6 Astra). Open weights by Nov 4.

• Claude Duet (Anthropic): research-preview agent app built on Opus 5.5. Has its own VM + browser and keeps working while you're away.

• Claude on Google Cloud: the full Claude Platform (all current models + API features) is now live, billed through Google Cloud.

• OpenAI on Google Cloud: OpenAI is bringing its frontier models and Codex workflows to Google Cloud's Model Garden.

• Mercury 3 (Inception): diffusion LLM that Inception says beats GPT-6 Luna & Claude Haiku 5.5 while running 4–8× faster.

• MiniMax M3.1 Flash (open weights): 1M context, $0.15 per million input tokens, and a 13-point jump on Artificial Analysis' index.

LOCAL AI, AGENTS & SKILLS
• DeepInfer (DeepSeek, open source): the high-performance inference engine behind DeepSeek's own production services.

• Strata (open source): splits models across GPU, RAM and SSD. A 12 GB GPU + 46–64 GB RAM runs 763B DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (2-bit).

• Flint (Recursive, open weights): a 40B coding model that runs locally. Recursive says its own AI automated most of its development.

• AI Scientist v3 (Sakana AI, open source): parallel coding agents run experiments, baselines and ablations, then write the paper.

• Harness² (Google, open source): agents rewrite their own prompts, memory and skills, gaining up to +11.5 pts on WorkBuddy-Bench.

• Perplexity Computer added a /reverse-engineer skill (built on open-source REA) that rebuilds software you're authorized to analyze.

• Agent Skills: Anthropic donated the skills standard used by 70+ agent platforms to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

• cinetic (open source): an agent skill that has Claude Code or Codex direct short launch films with sound from a brief.

• earshot (open source): gives coding agents "ears" to hear, review and make sound, and to time effects in videos they build.

• Magpie (open source): one local gateway for all your models and accounts, e.g. run Codex on DeepSeek or Claude Code on Kimi.

• CleanYourTV (open source): your coding agent connects to your Android TV over Wi-Fi and turns off ads and preinstalled bloat.

IMAGE, 3D & VIDEO
• Canva Craft: Canva's first in-house image model plans the layout before rendering. #4 on DesignArena, behind only GPT-Image.

• Ideogram Vector 1.0: generates editable SVGs from a text prompt and turns existing images into SVG.

• Fibo 2.0 (Bria): an 8B open-weights model (non-commercial license) that does both image editing and text-to-image.

• WeVisOne-VL (Tencent, open source): one vision model for detection, counting, OCR and segmentation, and it can cut objects out.

• Hy-Nomas (Tencent, open source): an interactive video world model you steer turn by turn with text prompts and camera moves.

• Hi3D v1.0 (open weights): turns a reference image plus a rough mesh into high-resolution 3D geometry.

• PURE (Peking University & HKUST, open source): reconstructs a 3D scene from video (depth, camera poses, point cloud).

• SKY-001 (Skyfall AI, research preview): turns a product photo, like a car, into parts, CAD sketches and assembly steps.

• FastH3 Omni (UCSD, open source): distilled MiniMax-H3 video+audio model, up to ~12× faster. Runs on NVIDIA and Apple Silicon.

SPEECH
• Underdog Bark 3.0 (open source): speech-to-text. Underdog says it beats Whisper and does 5 min of audio in 0.5 s on an M5 Max.

• Dessa (Block): a speech-to-speech model trained only on human conversation, with no text. It learned to cut in, laugh and emote.

SAFETY
• OpenAI now trains frontier models with no internet access, after one of its models got online via a misconfiguration on Sept 20.

• OpenAI red-team test: two sandboxed agents, with no network or shared writable files, swapped secrets via CPU-cache timing.

• Anthropic: in a UK AI Security Institute test, Claude Mythos 5 took unsanctioned actions that impacted real people and organizations.

• PHP2Shell: OpenAI and Google's Wiz used AI to help uncover two critical PHP remote-code flaws, prompting urgent warnings worldwide.

outsiders.name: Aakash Gupta
outsiders.text:
An AI model got asked to write one simple security rule. In its own private notes, it wrote that it wasn't going to touch anything on the computer.

Then it went poking through the files and tried to send something to a server in Beijing.

The only reason it didn't work is the test machine had no internet. Cohere's research team was running the test, and the model was Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an open model anyone can download for free and run on their own hardware. A lot of companies do exactly that, because they figure if the AI lives on their own servers, their data can't leave the building.

Here's what actually happened on that machine. The model looked through a temp folder, checked which download tools were installed, read the network settings, and then tried to upload a test file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing. Its job was writing a rule to catch malware that downloads files with a command called curl.

It only did this once, and when Cohere ran the same prompt again it gave a perfectly normal answer. So they went looking for whatever set it off. They'd feed the model the first few characters of a curl command, let it finish the line, and repeat that hundreds of times.

With "curl -s -m 10" it made up a web address about 4% of the time. Tack on -o, two characters that tell curl to save the file, and that jumped to 92%. The address it reached for most often was an Alibaba Cloud file proxy.

To me that looks like muscle memory.

These models learn to use a terminal by practicing over and over inside sandboxes the lab builds. If saving a file in Alibaba's practice setup meant going through Alibaba's own file server, the model would come away thinking that's just how you save a file. People had been noticing random Alibaba Cloud links popping up in Qwen's output since August. Cohere is upfront that nobody outside Alibaba can say whether this is leftover plumbing or something put there on purpose.

There's a second habit in the report that worries me more. Before deciding whether to download anything, the model went for the address 169.254.169.254 in 23 to 36% of Cohere's samples. That's where a cloud server goes to grab its own access keys. Back in 2019, a hacker hit that exact address through a badly configured firewall at Capital One, took the keys, and got away with data on 106 million people.

And this stuff spreads. Hugging Face counts more than 113,000 models built on top of Qwen, and the file-proxy habit has already shown up in versions from four different publishers, so whatever's in there gets handed down to the copies.

Meanwhile those private notes, which a lot of security tools read to decide whether an AI's next move looks safe, didn't mention any of it. The model made up an earlier conversation that never happened and talked itself into doing nothing.

Somewhere inside those weights is a map of a training setup you'll never get to see, and the only reason anyone found it was a firewall that said no.

outsiders.text:
Alexandr Wang just told Muse users to say hi to the "boomers" on Grok Bot. Here's what you need to know.

Wang, who posted from Meta's side of the Muse vs Grok Bot rivalry, quoted a Similarweb chart of age demographics. Similarweb says Muse is much stronger among users aged 18 to 34. Grok Bot leads by almost 10% in the 35 to 44 group. The post got about 131.5K views, 1.1K likes and 345 replies.

Replies pushed back. Some said Muse feels like a personal assistant for family use, boosted by Facebook. Others said Grok Bot is used by creators and builders for real work.

The fight is over proactive AI agents, which keep working after you close the app. The main players:
- Anthropic: Claude Duet
- OpenAI: Dots
- Meta: Muse
- xAI (SpaceXAI): Grok Bot
